newsitem.title: USA: NASD seeks comment on bond fund risk ratings idea.
newsitem.headline: NASD seeks comment on bond fund risk ratings idea.

text.p: The NASD said Tuesday it wants comments by February 24 on whether it should continue to bar the use of bond mutual fund risk ratings in sales literature given to customers.
Standard & Poor's Ratings Group in 1994 launched a service to rate the risk of bond funds, including municipal funds.
But the National Association of Securities Dealers, which regulates mutual fund advertising, ruled that funds may not use risk ratings in supplemental sales literature.

NASD worried that such ratings could mislead investors because they hinge on "assumptions and speculation" about the economy in general and about a company's solvency, management style, investment policy and portfolio changes, future dividend streams and rates of return.

The association's decision disappointed the Securities and Exchange Commmission which has been pushing for better disclosure by mutual funds of the sensitivity of their portfolios to changing market conditions.
S&P had assigned nearly 100 ratings to funds totaling $23 billion when NASD announced its position.
The NASD in a five-page request for comments released today outlined pros and cons of bond fund ratings.

On the positive side, NASD said investors do, indeed, need information to make informed decisions about their investments. And investors should be able to judge the usefulness of ratings when sales documents fully and fairly disclose material information about a fundm NASD said.

The SEC encourages "forward-looking" information in filings with the commission, NASD added. In fact, one SEC rule protects firms from liability if their projections are made reasonably and in good faith, NASD said.
On the negative side, NASD said that not all bond funds will buy ratings, giving those that do purchase the service an unfair marketing advantage.
"If a fund disagrees with a rating or does not wish to make a rating known publicly, it may opt not to obtain or reveal the rating," NASD said.
NASD asked whether such "selective availability" of ratings would create an "unfair built-in market bias in favor of funds that purchase a rating."
NASD also worries that funds may not carefully explain to buyers the methods rating agencies use to rate risk.
"In some instances, the...rating is in the form of a single word, symbol, or number (which may) provide little useful information to investors," NASD said.
NASD said it also is concerned that some salespeople will misuse ratings.
"Brokers may focus an investor's attention inappropriately on a risk rating as the key factor in the decision-making process," NASD said.
Comments should be mailed to Joan Conley, Office of the Corporate Secretary, NASD Regulation, Inc., 1735 K St., N.W., Washington, D.C. 20006-1500.
